newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African farm group upset at Hanekom remarks.
newsitem.headline: S.African farm group upset at Hanekom remarks.

text.p: The Transvaal Agricultural Union said on Wednesday it was disappointed at recent statements by Land Affairs and Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom, saying the two portfolios should not be held by the same minister.

"The department of land affairs has an out-and-out political agenda which must deliver on the African National Congress election promises," said a statement from the union, which represents mainly white farmers.
"In contrast, the department of agriculture has the responsibility of providing food, and along with that of the creation of jobs for hundreds of thousands of people," the union said.
It said Hanekom, in an interview with Reuters earlier in the week, had shown a lack of balance in his approach to the two portfolios and a failure to understand the agriculture industry.
"The union believes the minister is not qualified to handle the agriculture portfolio and urges the president (Nelson Mandela) to give priority attention to this situation," the statement said.
Among other things, Hanekom said market forces should be allowed to prevail in agriculture.
"My own view is that there shouldn't be any provision for drought relief for farmers... A crop failure you can expect from year to year and you have to provide for that as a farmer," Hanekom said.

"I'm a strong supporter of a move towards lower input agriculture, less chemical use," Hanekom said. "At the same time people are farming for profit and the reason some countries did really well in addressing major food deficiencies was the introduction of technology."
On land reform, he said the government would spend money "for a number of years" to give blacks access to land, "but not forever."
"You have to deal with the inequalities in the distribution of land, and once you've dealt with that, you don't subsidise the transfer of land forever...
"If you take it as a thumbsuck figure, I would say... These special land grants could go on for a 20-year period," Hanekom said.
